author: Autodesk
description: Procedurally construct a centipede skeleton with a spine and legs, then compute its animation in two steps. First, solve the spine animation by  driving it from the head and applying inextensibility is applied on it. Then, solve all legs animation by feeding them in an IK solver, and drive the IK target procedurally using a target blending mechanism.

metadata.author: Autodesk
metadata.description: Procedurally construct a centipede skeleton with a spine and legs, then compute its animation in two steps. First, solve the spine animation by  driving it from the head and applying inextensibility is applied on it. Then, solve all legs animation by feeding them in an IK solver, and drive the IK target procedurally using a target blending mechanism.

_notes.text: Procedurally compute the centipede skeleton's joint data. We initiate by computing the spine joint data, followed by leg data which is appended on global arrays. This data is then used to construct the actual skeleton object. Detailed explanations on the computation process are available in the compounds below.

Create a transform matrix with its position circulating arround the origin clockwise. You can play with ***Rotation speed*** and ***Circle radius*** values to change the target animation. Alternativelly, you could use the transform from an object inputed from the DCC application.

Solve each leg animation by using an inverse kinematic solver and procedurally computed IK target positions. A mechanism is used to determinate if a leg should lift or stay grounded, and another one is used to perform blending between ground and goal positions when a leg is lifted.

The computed matrices and their corresponding indices are used to update all of the skeleton's joint transforms using ***transform_joints***. Since we are solving the world matrices directly, the update method is set to ***From World*** here as well.

Create a plane mesh and deform it using the ***fractal_turbulence_field***. Then, build an accelerator in order to perform raycast queries inside the ***solve_spine_animation*** and ***solve_legs_animation*** compounds.

Solve the spine joints animation by applying inextensibility using the **Follow The Leader** method and conform the spine joint position to the terrain by doing raycasting. Then, recompute the orientation of the joints based on their positions.

The computed matrices and their corresponding indices are used to update all of the skeleton's joint transforms using ***transform_joints***. Since we are computing the result world matrices directly, the update method is set to ***From World***.

Update the ***chain_joint_indices*** geo property. This is a 2D array, where each sub-array contains all the indices of a given chain in order. 

In this example graph, it is used to operate on the spine and leg chains individually.

Create an array of pivot matrices that represents the skeleton's spine.

Additionally, we calculate their orientation ensuring the secondary joint rotation axis (***Y*** in this case) faces Z+. This orientation facilitates applying the procedural animation predominantly around this axis in subsequent steps.

Calculate the parent indices for the spine joints. Given that the spine joints are initially set in the skeleton, we designate the first value as the ***invalid_index***, marking it as the root joint. For the following joints, we set the values as ***current_index - 1***, ensuring that each joint's predecessor in the array serves as its parent.

When calculating both arms on the same hierarchy level, we aim for the left and right legs to share the same parent spine joint. This is achieved by dividing the ***current_index*** by two, ensuring the two legs of of the same level shares the same parent joint.

Additionally, when determining legs positions and orientations, the sign (+/-) varies based on the side we're working on. Hence, we employ a modulo operation to alternate between the right and left sides.

Then, tesize the feedback ***Previous_spine_world_matrices*** array if the joint count changes. If it skrinks, we just trim the data that we don't need. If it grows, we fill the new elements by the pivot matrices which represent the joint rest transforms.

First, replace the last spine joint by the ***head_target***. Then, apply inextensibility on the spine chain using the **Follow The Leader** algorithm. 

During each loop iteration, we move the current joint's parent joint transform either toward or away from its child depending on the distance between them and the ***spine_joint_interval_length*** value. The process is repeated sequentially until we reach the root of the spine.
